sections.h2: What is a deed of trust in Texas?
sections.html:
A deed of trust is the document most Texas homeowners sign to secure a mortgage loan, and it usually gives the lender a power of sale. If the borrower defaults, the lender can sell the home at a public auction without going to court first.

The loan itself is the promissory note. The deed of trust is the lien paper that ties the house to that note. When the note is paid off, the lender releases the lien, and that release is lodged in the clerk's office so the public record shows the house is free of that debt.

Texas law recognizes three routes to foreclose. The State Law Library describes them this way:

  • Judicial foreclosure, which goes through a lawsuit and is uncommon in Texas.
  • Nonjudicial foreclosure, which relies on the power of sale in the deed of trust and is governed by Property Code section 51.002.
  • Expedited foreclosure, which needs a court order and is the required route for home equity loans, reverse mortgages and some owners' association assessment liens.

sections.h2: How does nonjudicial foreclosure work under a deed of trust?
sections.html:
It works through a series of written notices followed by an auction, with no judge deciding whether the sale goes ahead. Because no court is involved, the notice deadlines in the statute carry most of the weight for the borrower.

For most home loans, a federal rule bars a servicer from starting foreclosure until the loan is more than 120 days delinquent. After that, the servicer sends a notice of default. The borrower can bring the loan current by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving that notice, under section 51.002(d).

If the default is not cured, the servicer then sends a notice of sale. It must go out three weeks or more ahead of the auction, with a copy on the courthouse door and another lodged with the clerk. Read each letter the day it arrives, because the dates printed on it set the schedule.

sections.h2: When and where is a Texas deed of trust foreclosure sale held?
sections.html:
Auctions are open to the public and happen on a month's first Tuesday during daytime hours. January 1 and July 4 are the exceptions, when the first Wednesday takes over, based on informal Attorney General guidance.

Start time is whatever the notice says, with a three-hour outer limit. Each commissioners court names the sales area and records it, so the clerk can tell you where bidding will happen.

sections.h2: How do the note and the deed of trust differ for a seller?
sections.html:
The note is the promise to repay, and the deed of trust is the security that lets the lender enforce it against the house. A seller usually needs a payoff statement from the servicer, and a title company will confirm that the lien is released when the loan is paid at closing.

Sellers whose house is in default often ask what a buyer can do. A buyer who pays off the loan before the auction gets a house whose lien is cleared in the record. After an auction, the buyer instead receives a trustee's deed recorded by the county clerk.

The same clerk records every instrument, so a title search shows each deed of trust, release and foreclosure notice in order. Reading that chain is the quickest way to see who holds a lien on the home and whether any paper is missing.

sections.h2: What happens after a deed of trust sale?
sections.html:
The winning bidder takes the property, and the former owner may still owe money. The lender can file a deficiency suit if the sale price fell short of the debt, but the clock is two years from the sale date. A borrower can ask the court to credit the home's fair market value against what is claimed.

If the sale brings in more than the debt, the extra money goes first to junior lienholders and then to the former owner. Texas does not give an automatic right to buy the house back after this kind of sale. Redemption rights exist only for certain situations, such as particular tax liens and owners' association assessment liens.

A buyer who finds the former owner still living in the house may need to file an eviction case to get possession. The notice and court steps for that are covered on the eviction pages of this site.

sections.h2: How is a deed of trust recorded and released with the county clerk?
sections.html:
Recording belongs to the county clerk, who serves as county recorder for deed records. A deed of trust, its release, and a trustee's deed after a sale all land in that same record.

To be recorded, an instrument that conveys real property needs a signature plus an acknowledgment, or an oath before two subscribing witnesses or an officer authorized to take acknowledgments, under Property Code section 12.001(b). The 2023 county clerk manual lists the standard fees:

  • A $5.00 charge for page one, then $4.00 for every added page or attachment.
  • $0.25 for each name over five that must be indexed.
  • A records management and preservation fee of no more than $10 and a records archive fee of no more than $10.
  • A records technology and infrastructure fee of $2.00.

Fees can change, so ask the county clerk for the current schedule before you file. After a loan is paid, confirm that the release of the deed of trust shows up in the clerk's index.

sections.h2: What can a Texas homeowner do when a deed of trust loan is in default?
sections.html:
The most direct option is to act inside the 20-day reinstatement window and ask the servicer for the exact payoff figure needed to cure. Missing that window does not end every option, but the later steps are tied to the sale calendar.

These are the main paths people weigh:

  • Bring the loan current with a reinstatement payment.
  • Ask the servicer about a repayment plan or loan modification before the sale date.
  • Sell the house before the first Tuesday sale so the proceeds pay off the lender and any remaining equity stays with you.
  • Speak with a Texas attorney or a legal aid office about your specific notice.

A sale before the auction date generally leaves a cleaner record than a foreclosure, because the lien is paid and released rather than enforced. Gather the notice of default, the notice of sale, and your loan statements first, since any buyer or lender will ask for them.

faqs.q: Does Texas require a court order to foreclose on a deed of trust?
faqs.a: Usually no. Nonjudicial foreclosure under the power of sale in the deed of trust does not need a court order. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and certain owners' association assessment liens need an expedited court order instead.

faqs.q: What is the cure period after a notice of default?
faqs.a: Twenty days from receipt. Paying the overdue amount in that span reinstates the loan under Property Code section 51.002(d). Ask the servicer for a written reinstatement figure so the amount is exact.

faqs.q: Can a Texas foreclosure sale happen on any day?
faqs.a: No. Sales are set for a month's first Tuesday, or the first Wednesday when January 1 or July 4 is that Tuesday. The notice gives a start time, and bidding has to begin within three hours of it.

faqs.q: Can I still owe money after the house is sold at auction?
faqs.a: Yes, possibly. A deficiency suit is allowed for two years after the sale, and you may ask for a credit based on the home's fair market value. Surplus sale money goes to junior liens first and then to the former owner.

faqs.q: Where do I find recorded deeds of trust and releases in Texas?
faqs.a: Search the clerk's records for the property's home county. The clerk records deeds of trust, releases, trustee's deeds and foreclosure sale notices, and charges the filing fees set by statute.
